k-1.x_notes: Strengths: ten problems with a good ramp. Pictured piles to circle or cross out for 1-5 and 10-12 (all correct: cross out 3 and 12, take 1 from 4 and 10, take 2 from 5 and 11). First-or-second choices for 6-9 (2nd, 1st, 1st, 2nd). A trap strip for 1-20 (multiples of 3). A greedy test, 'Ben always starts by taking 2', which works only for 5, 8 and 11, so the contrast with 4, 7 and 10 is built in. Listing every way a 4-game and a 5-game can go (5 and 8 ways, with spare rows so the count is not given away). Traps for {1,2,3} (multiples of 4). Two-pile choices including the non-obvious 1+4 (second wins) and a mirror-strategy question with 6+6. Misere traps (1,4,7,...). Shared rules are stated once and each task is a short, clear action, with large usable pictures and strips. Weaknesses: it never explicitly says to play with counters, so the adult has to start the hands-on play. Problems 7-10 will be a stretch for kindergartners. The footer has no ID.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: concrete, with explicit play from 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 counters and swapping starters. The mathematics is correct. Weaknesses: only six thin problems, so it will likely run out. It prints the strategy outright ('make two groups of 3', 'choose your reply so that exactly 3 counters remain', 'take enough to remove 3 counters between your two turns'), which removes the discovery. Problem 3 (a pile of 3) is trivial. The full rules are repeated in three problems. Tables and writing out move sequences are a burden for kindergartners. There are no pictures, and nothing on rule changes, greedy play or two piles. This matches the organizer's complaint that K-1 work is too dumbed down and ends too early.
k-1.reason: X gives K-1 real trap-hunting with contrasting cases, a greedy test and two-pile and misere variations, all on usable pictures. Y is thin, gives away the take-to-a-multiple-of-3 strategy, and will run out early.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: closely tied to the outline. Claim-testing problems are correct and well chosen: Lee's 12-counter complementing claim is right, Mo's 'take 2 from 10' is wrong, Jo's 10 to 7 under {1,3,4} is right (7 is losing), and Kai's 12 to 8 is wrong (8 is winning). Problem 3 requires answering every reply. Problem 4 classifies 1-20 under {1,3,4} (losing piles 2, 7, 9, 14, 16), and Problem 5 extends to 30, 50, 61 and 100 (second, first take 1, first take 3, second). Problem 6 covers {1,3,5} parity with an explanation, and Problem 7 has two-pile cases including 4+1 being a second-player win. Problem 8 is an inverse design problem: losing piles at multiples of 5 force {1,2,3,4}, and a different rule needs an extra move such as 6. The intro is concise, there are generous work spaces, and each problem is open about method. Weaknesses: there is no explicit instruction to play with counters first, and it is ambitious enough that the group will not finish. The footer has no ID.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: it starts concretely by playing {1,3,4} from 5, 6 and 7. Problem 4 (play an L pile against every first move) matches the outline's 'test strategies against every reply'. The mathematics is correct (8 is W with take 1; from 10, take 1 or 3). Weaknesses: it is broken into tiny directed steps (Problem 2 on piles of 2 and 4 is trivial, and Problems 5 and 6 are three-row tables). Problem 3 prints the backward-induction rule as a procedure ('Mark W if at least one is L'). The rules are repeated in several problems, with fussy directions ('Reset each time', 'a partner may write while you play'). It stops at pile 10, with no pattern, rule change or claims to judge.
grades-2-3.reason: X has third graders judging concrete strategy claims, classifying piles, extending to large piles and changing the rule, with open method. Y is correct but turns the same idea into small, procedure-driven table fills that stop early.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: rich and well sequenced. It classifies {1,3,4} for 1-24, then 100, 1000 and 2026 (losing, take 4, take 3 or 1). It compares {1,2}, {1,2,4}, {1,4} and {1,3,5} (period 3, the same period 3, mod 5 in {0,2}, and parity), which is a good surprise. A greedy-plan analysis follows: it fails at 4, 5 and 8 respectively and works for {1,3,5}. Then come an explanation of why the pattern continues forever, and an inverse problem with a completeness proof ({1,2,3} plus any subset of {5,6}, so four games). Misere versions are shifted by one, then come two-pile grids for {1,2} and {1,3,4}; the latter's unequal losing pairs (1,3), (1,8), (3,8), (2,7) and (4,6) exist and are findable. Everything checks. The task statements are concise and leave method open, with good grids. Weaknesses: it opens with abstract classification and no explicit play. There is more than three children will finish. The 9x9 two-pile grid is heavy by hand. The footer has no ID.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: a concrete start (play 8, 10, 14) and a coherent, correct path to period 7 for {1,3,4}. The window rule (inspect cells 1, 2 and 4) is correct and points toward the pigeonhole idea, and children will be busy. Weaknesses: it prints the discoveries. The chart is laid out in rows of 7 with 'compare the rows', Problem 5 says to arrange counters in groups of 7, and Problem 9 hands over the window procedure. It is mostly table-filling in small steps, and Problem 6's directions are confusing ('use piles 7 and 9 so that all three moves are possible'). The rules are repeated. Comparing rules is reduced to one small {1,3,5} box, with no greedy idea, two piles or other rules, so it is weak on the outline's 'compare what happens when the rule changes'.
grades-4-5.reason: X develops patterns across several rules, a greedy counterexample, a periodicity proof and an inverse problem with open method. Y walks one rule to period 7 by printing the grouping-by-sevens and window procedures, which removes the discovery.

overall.reason: X is better in every band. It uses correct, substantial and well-contrasted problems in the organizer's format, with rules stated once and tasks clear but open; its defects (adding a 'play it with counters' nudge, footer IDs) are quick edits. Y repeats rules, breaks investigations into tiny table steps and prints the key strategies and patterns, and its K-1 pages are thin. Fifteen minutes per band cannot fix that.
